script.title: How to file your freelance tax return, step by step
script.hook: Filing your own freelance tax return can feel like a black box. You answer questions, numbers appear, and you hope they're right. In this video we'll file a twenty twenty-six return for one example freelancer, from the pile of paperwork to the confirmation email, in the order you'd actually do it. Federal rules, twenty twenty-six figures.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Filing your own freelance tax return can feel like a black box. You answer questions, numbers appear, and you hope they're right. In this video we'll file a twenty twenty-six return for one example freelancer, from the pile of paperwork to the confirmation email, in the order you'd actually do it. Whether you use software, a professional, or a mix, knowing this order means you'll catch mistakes and you'll know what every number means. Education, not tax advice. Federal rules, twenty twenty-six figures.
segments.on_screen_text: Filing a freelance return, start to finish
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes opening a folder full of neat papers. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Meet Sam
segments.narration: Meet Sam, a fictional freelance designer and a single filer. In twenty twenty-six, clients paid Sam sixty-eight thousand five hundred dollars. Sam's business expenses, including a home office and mileage, came to eight thousand five hundred. So Sam's profit is sixty thousand. Sam paid nine thousand dollars in estimated tax during the year, has no other job, and uses the standard deduction. Keep those numbers in mind; we'll use them all the way through.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with a pencil and coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step one
segments.narration: Step one is gathering. You want every ten ninety-nine NEC and ten ninety-nine K you received, your own income log for the year, your expense totals by category, your mileage log total, your home office measurements, and a record of every estimated payment you made, with dates. Download that last one from your IRS online account rather than trusting memory. Also have last year's return open; it's the best checklist you own, because most of this year's forms will look like last year's.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tidy stack of forms, a notebook and a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step two
segments.narration: Step two is matching income. Add up what your ten ninety-nines say and compare it with your income log. They won't match exactly, and that's normal. Clients under the reporting threshold may not send a form at all. A payment sent at the very end of December may appear in a different year. Platforms report gross amounts before fees. What matters is that you report everything you were actually paid in twenty twenty-six, and that you can explain any difference if asked. Sam's log says sixty-eight thousand five hundred, so that's gross receipts.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two lists with lines connecting matching rows. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step three
segments.narration: Step three is choosing how to file. If your year was simple, one business, no employees, no property sales, software handles it well. Some low-cost options file Schedule C federally at no charge. If you had a big unusual event, several states, or an S corporation, a professional is usually worth it. There's also a middle path: do it yourself in software and pay for a one-time review. Whichever you choose, the steps from here are the same.
segments.on_screen_text: Step 3: DIY, software or a pro
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three doors with small signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step four
segments.narration: Step four is Schedule C, the heart of the return. Enter gross receipts, then expenses by category: software, equipment, advertising, phone and internet for the business share, professional fees, supplies, and so on. Then the car: Sam drove four thousand business miles, and at seventy-two and a half cents a mile that's two thousand nine hundred dollars. Then the home office: Sam's two hundred square foot office at the simplified rate of five dollars a square foot is one thousand dollars. All in, Sam's expenses total eight thousand five hundred, so Schedule C profit is sixty thousand.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with columns filling in. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step five
segments.narration: Step five is self-employment tax, on Schedule SE. Software does this automatically, but here's what happens. Multiply profit by ninety-two point three five percent: that's fifty-five thousand four hundred and ten dollars. Multiply that by fifteen point three percent: self-employment tax of about eight thousand four hundred and seventy-eight dollars. Half of it, about four thousand two hundred and thirty-nine, is deductible later. This is the tax that surprises new freelancers the most, and it's why freelancers owe more than employees on the same income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pie with one slice highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step six
segments.narration: Step six is adjustments to income, on Schedule one. That deductible half of self-employment tax goes here. So would self-employed health insurance premiums, contributions to a SEP or a traditional IRA, and student loan interest. Sam only has the self-employment tax deduction, so adjusted gross income is sixty thousand minus four thousand two hundred and thirty-nine: fifty-five thousand seven hundred and sixty-one dollars. Write this number down. Next year, it decides whether your safe harbor is a hundred or a hundred and ten percent.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a small slice removed. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step seven
segments.narration: Step seven is deductions. Sam takes the standard deduction, sixteen thousand one hundred dollars for a single filer in twenty twenty-six. Then the qualified business income deduction, on Form eighty-nine ninety-five: generally twenty percent of business income, but limited to twenty percent of taxable income before the deduction. For Sam that limit bites, so the deduction is about seven thousand nine hundred and thirty-two. Taxable income comes out at thirty-one thousand seven hundred and twenty-nine dollars.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two blocks being lifted off a stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step eight
segments.narration: Step eight is the tax itself. On thirty-one thousand seven hundred and twenty-nine of taxable income, a single filer's income tax is about three thousand five hundred and fifty-nine dollars, using the twenty twenty-six brackets. Add the self-employment tax of eight thousand four hundred and seventy-eight, and Sam's total federal tax is about twelve thousand and thirty-seven dollars. That's about twenty percent of profit. It's the number on the total tax line, and it's the most important number on the whole return.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a large coin with a small label. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step nine
segments.narration: Step nine is payments and the balance. Sam paid nine thousand dollars in estimated tax. Enter each payment, and check the total against your IRS online account, because a mismatch here is one of the most common reasons for a letter. Twelve thousand and thirty-seven minus nine thousand leaves a balance due of about three thousand and thirty-seven. If Sam had paid more than the total tax, there'd be a refund instead, and Sam could choose to apply it to twenty twenty-seven's first estimated payment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin labeled with a small arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step ten
segments.narration: Step ten is the penalty check. Software will ask whether you owe an underpayment penalty, on Form twenty-two ten. Sam's twenty twenty-five total tax was eight thousand dollars, and Sam paid nine thousand on time across four quarters. That beats a hundred percent of last year's tax, so the safe harbor applies and there's no penalty, even with a balance due. If you missed payments, or paid late, the software works out the penalty. If most of your income came late in the year, try the annualized method before you accept it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield with a check mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step eleven
segments.narration: Step eleven is the review. Before you submit, compare the return with last year's, line by line, and ask why each big change happened. Check your name, Social Security number and bank details. Check the business code and address. Check that gross receipts are at least the total of your ten ninety-nines. Check the estimated payments match your IRS account. And read the summary of the state return too, if your state taxes income. Ten minutes here saves months of letters later.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a magnifying glass over two forms side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step twelve
segments.narration: Step twelve is filing and paying. E-file, and choose how to pay the balance: a direct debit with the return on a date you pick, or IRS Direct Pay later, choosing balance due and the twenty twenty-six tax year. Both are free. Then, on the same day or soon after, pay the first estimated payment for twenty twenty-seven. Using the safe harbor, that's twelve thousand and thirty-seven divided by four: about three thousand and ten dollars. Two payments, two tax years, both due April fifteenth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coins dropping into two slots. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: After
segments.narration: After you file, save a PDF of the full return, the confirmation, and the payment receipts in one folder for the year. Copy five numbers somewhere you'll see them: total tax, adjusted gross income, Schedule C profit, estimated payments made, and the refund or balance due. Then work out your real rate: Sam's total tax divided by profit is about twenty percent. Add your state rate and a small cushion. That's what Sam sets aside from every client payment in twenty twenty-seven.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a folder labeled with a year and a sticky note. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Gather, match income, choose how to file, fill in Schedule C, then Schedule SE, then adjustments, deductions and the tax. Enter payments, check for a penalty, review against last year, file and pay twice. Save the return and set next year's percentage. script.title: Owe the IRS more than you expected? Every option, explained
script.hook: You finish your return, and the balance due is bigger than the money you set aside. It's one of the most stressful moments in freelancing, and it happens to a lot of people in their first or second year. The good news is that the IRS has more options than most people think, and the worst move is doing nothing. In this video we'll go through every option, in the order you should consider them, with what each one costs. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: You finish your return, and the balance due is bigger than the money you set aside. It's one of the most stressful moments in freelancing, and it happens to a lot of people in their first or second year. The good news is that the IRS has more options than most people think, and the worst move is doing nothing. In this video we'll go through every option, in the order you should consider them, with what each one costs. Education, not tax advice.
segments.on_screen_text: Owe more than you can pay?
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes looking at a long receipt with wide eyes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why
segments.narration: First, why it happens, so it doesn't happen twice. Usually it's one of three things. Income grew during the year and the set-aside didn't. Estimated payments were skipped when money was tight. Or self-employment tax came as a surprise, because nobody mentioned the fifteen point three percent. Whatever the reason, write it down. We'll fix it at the end of the video.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small signposts. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rule one
segments.narration: Rule one: file on time, even if you can't pay a cent. The penalty for filing late is five percent of the unpaid tax for every month or part of a month, up to twenty-five percent. The penalty for paying late is half a percent a month. Filing late is ten times more expensive. If your return truly isn't ready, file an extension by April fifteenth, but pay what you can with it, because the extension doesn't extend the time to pay.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tall bar and a short bar side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rule two
segments.narration: Rule two: pay as much as you can by April fifteenth. Interest and the late-payment penalty are charged on the unpaid balance, so every dollar you pay now stops costing you. If you can pay most of it, do. Raid the savings that aren't your emergency fund before reaching for anything expensive.
segments.on_screen_text: Rule 2: pay what you can now
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. coins dropping into a slot. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Short
segments.narration: Option one is a short-term payment plan. If you can pay the full amount within a hundred and eighty days, you can usually set one up online in your IRS account. There's no setup fee for the short-term plan, though interest and the late-payment penalty keep running until it's paid. For a lot of freelancers, this is all you need: a few months of client payments clears it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with six small coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Long
segments.narration: Option two is a long-term installment agreement: monthly payments over a longer period. Individuals who owe up to fifty thousand dollars in combined tax, penalties and interest can generally apply online. There's a setup fee, lower if you pay by direct debit, and lower still for low-income applicants. While the plan is active, the late-payment penalty drops to a quarter of a percent a month, as long as you filed on time. Interest still applies.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with many small coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Card
segments.narration: Option three is a credit card. You can pay the IRS by card through approved processors, who charge a fee. The real cost is the card's interest rate if you can't clear it, which is usually far higher than the IRS's interest plus penalty. A card only makes sense if you can pay it off within the grace period, or you have a genuine zero percent offer and a plan to clear it before it ends.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a card with a warning sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Loan
segments.narration: Option four is a personal loan or borrowing from family. It can be cheaper than a card, but compare it honestly with an IRS installment agreement, which is often cheaper than people expect. Avoid borrowing from a retirement account. Early withdrawals usually add income tax and a ten percent penalty, and you'll be in the same position next year with less saved.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coin stacks compared. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Relief
segments.narration: Option five is penalty relief. If you have a clean record, meaning no penalties in the previous three years and all required returns filed, you may qualify for first-time penalty relief on the failure to file or failure to pay penalties. You can ask for it after you've paid, or with the IRS when you set up a plan. It doesn't remove interest on the tax itself, but it can remove a meaningful chunk. There's also reasonable-cause relief for things like serious illness or disasters.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield with a small star. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Hardship
segments.narration: Option six is for real hardship. If paying anything would leave you unable to cover basic living expenses, you can ask the IRS to mark your account as currently not collectible, which pauses collection, though interest continues. And an offer in compromise lets some people settle for less than they owe, based on their income, expenses and assets. Most applications don't qualify, and you should be wary of anyone advertising that they can settle your debt for pennies. The IRS has a free pre-qualifier tool.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small hand holding a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Letters
segments.narration: Whatever you choose, expect letters. If you don't pay in full, the IRS will send a series of notices, each a little firmer. Read every one. They tell you the current balance, including interest, and what happens next. Respond by the date on the letter. Most collection trouble starts not with the debt but with ignored mail. If you've set up a plan, the letters should stop or confirm the plan.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an envelope with a calendar date. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Don't forget your state. If you owe the state too, most states have their own payment plans, and their penalties and interest can be steeper. Treat it as a second bill with its own plan, not something to deal with later.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a smaller second form with coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Example
segments.narration: Here's an example. Alex, a freelancer, owes four thousand two hundred dollars on April fifteenth and has one thousand two hundred available. Alex files on time, pays one thousand two hundred with the return, and sets up a short-term plan online to clear the remaining three thousand over the next three months from client payments. The penalty and interest on that come to tens of dollars, not hundreds. If Alex had filed three months late instead, the filing penalty alone would be hundreds.
segments.on_screen_text: Example: file, pay $1,200, plan the rest
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a timeline with three small coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Next year
segments.narration: Now, the fix for next year. Take your total tax from this return and divide it by your profit. That's your real rate. Add your state rate and a cushion, and move that share of every client payment into a separate tax account the day it lands. Pay quarterly using the safe harbor: last year's total tax divided by four. And if income jumps mid-year, raise the set-aside straight away, not in April.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar filling from every coin that arrives. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Online account
segments.narration: A practical tip before you choose. Make an IRS online account if you don't have one. It shows your balance, including penalties and interest as of today, every payment you've made and the year it went to, and the notices the IRS has sent. Many payment plans can be set up there in a few minutes, and you can change the monthly amount or the due date later if your income moves around, which matters when you're paid by clients rather than a salary.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop showing a simple balance. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Plan tips
segments.narration: Some tips for living with a plan. Choose a monthly amount you can pay even in a slow month, then pay extra when a big invoice lands; extra payments reduce interest. Pay by direct debit, which lowers the setup fee and means you won't miss one. And keep filing and paying your new estimated taxes on time. A plan can be cancelled if you fall behind on new taxes, and that's the most common way people lose one. Treat this year's quarterly payments as part of the plan.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with steady small coins and one big one. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pros
segments.narration: When should you get help? If you owe a large amount, have several years of unfiled returns, or have already received a final notice of intent to levy, talk to an enrolled agent, a CPA or a tax attorney. Low-income taxpayers may qualify for free help from a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic. And the Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent part of the IRS that can step in when a problem is causing real hardship or the normal channels aren't working.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small figure handing over a folder. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. File on time no matter what. Pay what you can now. Use a short-term plan if you can clear it in a hundred and eighty days, or an installment agreement if not. Be careful with cards and loans, and never raid retirement. Ask about first-time penalty relief. Read every letter. Handle the state too. Then fix the set-aside so it doesn't happen again. The free calculator and the Quarterly Tax Tracker are in the description. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: Still time to lower your 2026 tax: what works in March
script.hook: Most tax advice about cutting your bill comes in December. But for freelancers, a surprising amount can still be done in March and early April for last year's return, before you file. Some of it is new money into accounts with a deadline that hasn't passed. Some of it is deductions you already earned and forgot to claim. In this video, every legitimate move still open for twenty twenty-six, with what each one actually saves at sixty thousand dollars of profit. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Most tax advice about cutting your bill comes in December. But for freelancers, a surprising amount can still be done in March and early April for last year's return, before you file. Some of it is new money into accounts with a deadline that hasn't passed. Some of it is deductions you already earned and forgot to claim. In this video, every legitimate move still open for twenty twenty-six, with what each one actually saves at sixty thousand dollars of profit. Education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding a calendar with March circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Two kinds
segments.narration: First, an important difference. A business expense on Schedule C reduces both income tax and self-employment tax. At sixty thousand of profit, each thousand dollars of expenses saves a single filer about two hundred and thirty-one dollars of federal tax. A personal deduction, like an IRA or HSA contribution, reduces income tax only. At the same profit, each thousand saves about ninety-six dollars. Both are worth having, but finding missed business expenses is worth more than twice as much per dollar.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coin stacks of different heights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Missed expenses
segments.narration: So start with expenses you already paid for and haven't counted. Go through your bank and card statements for the whole year, line by line. Freelancers commonly miss software subscriptions billed annually, payment processing fees taken out before money reached them, the business share of a phone and internet bill, professional memberships, courses that maintain or improve skills for your current work, a portion of tax preparation fees, bank fees on the business account, and small equipment. Each needs a record and a real business purpose. Nothing here is new spending.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a statement with lines highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Home office
segments.narration: Next, the home office. If part of your home is used regularly and exclusively for your business, and it's your principal place of business, you can deduct it. The simplified method is five dollars a square foot, up to three hundred square feet, so up to fifteen hundred dollars. The regular method uses actual costs, like rent, utilities and insurance, by the share of your home the office takes up, and can be larger. A two hundred square foot office at the simplified rate is a thousand dollars of deductions, worth about two hundred and thirty dollars at sixty thousand of profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a desk in a small room with a ruler. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mileage
segments.narration: Then your car. Business driving, to clients, to pick up supplies, to a coworking space that isn't your regular office, counts at seventy-two and a half cents a mile for twenty twenty-six. Commuting to a regular workplace doesn't. If you don't have a log, you can rebuild one honestly from your calendar, emails, invoices and map history. Three thousand business miles is about two thousand one hundred and seventy-five dollars of deductions, worth about five hundred dollars of tax at sixty thousand.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a car on a road with mile markers. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health
segments.narration: Next, health insurance. If you paid for your own health insurance in twenty twenty-six and weren't eligible for an employer-subsidized plan, including through a spouse, in those months, the premiums are usually deductible as an adjustment to income. It doesn't reduce self-employment tax, but it reduces income tax, and you don't need to itemize. People forget it because the premiums came from a personal account. Five thousand dollars of premiums is worth around four hundred and eighty dollars at sixty thousand of profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small shield with a cross. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: IRA
segments.narration: Now the accounts with deadlines still open. A traditional IRA contribution for twenty twenty-six can be made until April fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven. The limit is seven thousand five hundred dollars, or eight thousand six hundred if you're fifty or older. If you don't have a workplace retirement plan, it's generally fully deductible. Tell the provider it's for twenty twenty-six. At sixty thousand of profit, the full seven thousand five hundred saves about seven hundred and twenty dollars. A Roth gives no deduction now, but tax-free growth, and at this income it's often the better long-term choice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with a coin and a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: HSA
segments.narration: If you had an HSA-eligible health plan in twenty twenty-six, you can still contribute to an HSA for that year until April fifteenth. The limit is four thousand four hundred dollars for self-only coverage and eight thousand seven hundred and fifty for family, plus a thousand if you're fifty-five or older, reduced for months you weren't covered. The money comes out tax-free for medical costs, and it can be invested and kept for decades. That's why many people consider it the best account there is.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with a small cross. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: SEP
segments.narration: The SEP IRA is the big one for freelancers. You can open and fund one for twenty twenty-six right up to your filing deadline, including an extension, so potentially until October fifteenth. A sole proprietor can contribute about twenty percent of net self-employment earnings. At sixty thousand of profit, that's up to about eleven thousand one hundred and fifty dollars, saving roughly one thousand and seventy dollars of federal tax. If you have employees, they generally need contributions at the same rate. Note that a SEP and an IRA can both be used for the same year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a large jar with a calendar arrow to October. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Credits
segments.narration: Then check credits, which reduce tax dollar for dollar. The saver's credit rewards retirement contributions for people with modest income; at some income levels, an IRA contribution earns both a deduction and a credit. The premium tax credit reconciles marketplace health insurance; make sure Form eighty-nine sixty-two is filed if you had a marketplace plan. And education credits may apply to courses that don't qualify as business expenses. Software asks about each, so answer carefully.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin with a small star. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: QBI
segments.narration: Make sure you got the qualified business income deduction. It's twenty percent of business income for most freelancers below about two hundred thousand dollars of taxable income, limited to twenty percent of taxable income. It's automatic in most software, but it's worth checking that Form eighty-nine ninety-five is there. Note that SEP contributions and the self-employed health insurance deduction reduce the business income it's based on.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a check mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Not
segments.narration: Now, what doesn't work in March. You can't buy equipment now and deduct it for twenty twenty-six. You can't prepay twenty twenty-seven expenses into last year. You can't count a client payment you received in January as twenty twenty-six income, or move a December invoice into this year. And you can't back-date anything. If someone suggests that, walk away. The banned version of tax planning is the one that ends in letters.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar page with a red cross. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Order
segments.narration: So in what order should you do this? First, the free stuff: find every missed business expense, the home office, mileage, and the health insurance deduction. Then decide how much cash you can put into accounts, and choose between an IRA, HSA and SEP based on what you have and what you'll need. If cash is tight, file an extension, pay your estimated tax by April fifteenth, and fund the SEP later in the year. Never pay the IRS late to fund an IRA.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a numbered list. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Example
segments.narration: Here's Sam again, sixty thousand of profit. Sam finds twelve hundred dollars of missed software and fees, claims the home office for a thousand, and adds two thousand one hundred and seventy-five of mileage. That's about four thousand four hundred of expenses, worth roughly a thousand dollars of tax. Then Sam puts three thousand into a traditional IRA for twenty twenty-six, saving about two hundred and ninety more. Around thirteen hundred dollars less tax, mostly from money Sam had already spent.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: One last thing before you claim any of this: keep the evidence. For missed expenses, save the statement line and a one-line note of the business purpose. For the home office, a measurement and a photo. For mileage, the rebuilt log and what you rebuilt it from. For contributions, the confirmation that says which year they're for. It takes an hour, and it turns every deduction from a hope into a record.

segments.narration: Recap. Business expenses save more than personal deductions, so start there: missed costs, the home office, mileage and health insurance. segments.heading: Payment one
segments.narration: Payment one is the balance due for twenty twenty-six. It's simple: total tax on your return, minus everything you've already paid toward twenty twenty-six. That means estimated payments, any withholding from a job, and any overpayment from twenty twenty-five that you applied forward. If the result is positive, that's what you owe by April fifteenth. If it's negative, it's a refund, which you can take or apply to twenty twenty-seven.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a subtraction. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Payment two
segments.narration: Payment two is the first estimated payment for twenty twenty-seven. You have three ways to work it out. The safe harbor: your twenty twenty-six total tax divided by four, or a hundred and ten percent of it divided by four if last year's adjusted gross income was over a hundred and fifty thousand. The current-year method: ninety percent of what you expect to owe for twenty twenty-seven, divided by four. Or the annualized method, if your income is very uneven. The safe harbor is the easiest, because you already know the number.

segments.heading: Sam
segments.narration: Example one: Sam, a single designer with sixty thousand of profit in twenty twenty-six. Total tax: about twelve thousand and thirty-seven. Sam paid nine thousand in estimates, so payment one is about three thousand and thirty-seven. Sam's adjusted gross income was about fifty-five thousand eight hundred, under a hundred and fifty thousand, so the safe harbor is a hundred percent: twelve thousand and thirty-seven divided by four is about three thousand and ten. On April fifteenth, Sam pays about six thousand and forty-seven dollars.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card and two coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Priya
segments.narration: Example two: Priya, a first-year freelancer, who left a salaried job in twenty twenty-six with tax withheld all year from the job's paychecks. Priya made thirty thousand of freelance profit on top. Priya's total tax is higher than what was withheld, so there's a balance. But because Priya had tax withheld evenly through the year, and the withholding covered last year's tax, there's no penalty. For twenty twenty-seven, with no job and no withholding, Priya pays estimates for the first time. The safe harbor is based on Priya's twenty twenty-six total tax, including the part covered by withholding.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with a briefcase and a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Priya numbers
segments.narration: Say Priya's twenty twenty-six total tax was eleven thousand, and the job withheld nine thousand five hundred. Payment one is fifteen hundred. The safe harbor for twenty twenty-seven is eleven thousand divided by four: two thousand seven hundred and fifty a quarter. But Priya now expects only thirty-five thousand of freelance profit for twenty twenty-seven, and no salary, so the tax will probably be lower. The current-year method may let Priya pay less each quarter, as long as it reaches ninety percent of the actual twenty twenty-seven tax.

segments.heading: Jordan
segments.narration: Example three: Jordan, a developer with a hundred and twenty thousand of profit, filing single. Jordan's total tax is about twenty-eight thousand four hundred and sixty-two. Jordan paid twenty-four thousand in estimates, so payment one is about four thousand four hundred and sixty-two. Jordan's adjusted gross income was about a hundred and eleven thousand five hundred, under the threshold, so the safe harbor is still a hundred percent: about seven thousand one hundred and sixteen a quarter. Jordan pays about eleven thousand five hundred and seventy-eight on April fifteenth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with code brackets. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Over 150
segments.narration: If Jordan had earned enough for adjusted gross income over a hundred and fifty thousand, the safe harbor would rise to a hundred and ten percent of last year's tax. That ten percent catches a lot of growing freelancers by surprise, because it arrives the year after a big jump in income. If your income is climbing, check your adjusted gross income line before you work out the first payment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin growing a little. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Separate
segments.narration: Now, how to pay. These must be two separate payments. In IRS Direct Pay or your online account, the first is reason balance due, tax year twenty twenty-six. The second is estimated tax, tax year twenty twenty-seven. Mix them up, and your twenty twenty-seven payment can land on your twenty twenty-six account, or the other way round, and you'll get letters about money you actually paid. If you e-file with a direct debit for the balance, you still make the estimated payment separately.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two slots with different labels. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Cash
segments.narration: What if paying both at once is too much? The first payment has the strict deadline: interest and the late-payment penalty start on April sixteenth. The estimated payment also matters, but a slightly late first quarter usually costs less than a late balance. Pay the balance, pay as much of the estimate as you can, and make up the rest quickly. Just don't skip it, because the safe harbor needs four on-time payments.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a balance scale. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rest
segments.narration: Now set up the rest of twenty twenty-seven. The other dates are June fifteenth, September fifteenth, and January eighteenth, twenty twenty-eight, because January fifteenth falls on a Saturday and the Monday after is a federal holiday. With the safe harbor, each payment is the same amount. You can schedule all of them now in your IRS online account or through EFTPS, so they happen even in a busy month.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with four flags. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Set-aside
segments.narration: And reset your set-aside. The safe harbor protects you from penalties, not from the bill. If you earn more in twenty twenty-seven, you'll owe the difference next April. So take your real rate from this return, total tax divided by profit, add your state rate and a cushion, and move that percentage of every client payment into a separate tax account. Sam's rate is about twenty percent federal; Jordan's is about twenty-four.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a dial being turned. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Your state may want two payments too. Many states require estimated payments from freelancers, and many use similar dates. Check your state's tax agency site for its safe harbor rules, which aren't always the same as the federal ones, and add those dates to the same calendar.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map pin with coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Refund
segments.narration: What if you're getting a refund instead? Then there's no payment one, and you have a choice. Take the refund as cash, or apply some or all of it to your twenty twenty-seven estimated tax. Applying it counts as paid on April fifteenth, so it can cover your first quarter entirely. If cash flow is tight, that's convenient. If you'd rather hold the money, take the refund and pay the first estimate yourself. Either way, a big refund means your set-aside was too high, so adjust it.

segments.heading: Extension
segments.narration: And if you're filing an extension? You still make both payments by April fifteenth. For payment one, estimate your twenty twenty-six balance as well as you can and pay it with the extension, because the extension only gives you until October fifteenth to file the paperwork. If you underestimate, interest and the late-payment penalty apply to the shortfall. For payment two, use your best estimate of twenty twenty-six total tax for the safe harbor, and adjust the later quarters once you've filed.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with an arrow to October and two coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Three mistakes to avoid on the day. Paying the estimate as a balance due, which credits it to the wrong year. Using last year's adjusted gross income threshold from memory instead of the return. And forgetting that a weekend or holiday deadline moves to the next business day, which is why January twenty twenty-eight's payment is on the eighteenth. Check each one, save both confirmations, and you're done until June.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Payment one: twenty twenty-six total tax minus what you paid. Payment two: twenty twenty-six total tax divided by four, or a hundred and ten percent if your adjusted gross income was over a hundred and fifty thousand. Pay them separately with the right type and year. Schedule June, September and January now. Reset your set-aside from your real rate.
